newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Colonial symbols disappear from Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Colonial symbols disappear from Hong Kong.

text.p: They were just five years old and starting school in 1984 when, with a stroke of the pen, then British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher signed Hong Kong over to China.
Thatcher put her signature to a Sino-British treaty promising to return the colony to China at midnight on June 30, 1997, a date then 13 years distant.
Now just weeks before the British fulfill their side of the bargain, those schoolchildren are young adults preparing to graduate from high school.
The class of 1997 at Hong Kong's elite King's College will be the last to study in classrooms adorned with the portrait of Britain's Queen Elizabeth.
The monarch's crown will disappear from the school badge at the end of the summer term to be replaced with a stylised logo representing a student reading a book.
A brisk secondary market has sprung up as King's College students and alumni rushed to buy old badges before the final page turned on Britain's colonial adventures in Asia.
"Fortunately, the school name will not be changed," said pupil Kenneth Tang, 18. "I like the school name and I don't want it to be changed."
Hong Kong has embarked on a wholescale purge of British symbols, icons and insignia but there are few plans to scrap colonial place names -- yet.
One exception is Victoria Park, named after the Queen reigning when a naval patrol planted the British flag on Hong Kong island in 1841. It will be renamed Hong Kong Central Park.
Work began last week on removing the Royal insignia from Hong Kong's 800 post boxes.

The Royal Mail, to be renamed Hong Kong Post, is taking the opportunity for a corporate revamp and will paint its red post vans and boxes a viridian green -- similar in hue to China's -- and adopt a humming bird logo.
Newly minted coins no longer carry the Queen's head. Her profile was removed from postage stamps earlier this year.
The Hong Kong Jockey Club has dropped its Royal prefix and the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club has begun the search for a new mainland patron to replace the Queen.
From July 1, China's five-starred flag will flutter in place of the red white and blue British flag.

The colonial flag -- a blue ensign incorporating the British flag and Hong Kong crest -- will be consigned to the history books and replaced with one depicting a stylised version of the Bauhinia flower -- a sterile hybrid also known as a tree orchid.
The drawdown of Britain's most obvious manifestation of sovereignty -- its garrison -- gathered pace last year.

The British military school has closed. The Gurkha regiments -- Nepali soldiers who serve the British crown -- marched into the sunset. Buyers were sought for its Wessex helicopters. The Navy's three Peacock class patrol ships will be sold to Manila.
China prepared to claim sovereignty last month when a Chinese army advance guard rolled across the border to ready facilities for the future Chinese garrison.
King's College student Shirley Sin, 18, said she would miss the colonial trappings. "But I'm also delighted to see the new challenges ahead."
Her classmate Tang may be glad to see the King's College name endure but he's also excited about the future.
"I feel happy about Hong Kong's return to China, because we are Chinese."
